seo.title: Karmic tail 21 19 16 compatibility: The World, The Sun, The Tower
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 19 16 compatibility: what The World, The Sun and The Tower mean for a couple who live in plain sight, and how to survive a fallen image.

title: Karmic tail 21-19-16 in compatibility: the bridal chorus and the forbidden question
short: In much of the world brides walk down the aisle to the bridal chorus from Wagner's Lohengrin, and few people remember where that chorus leads in the opera itself: to a bedroom where the marriage collapses that same night over a single question. Karmic tail 21-19-16 in compatibility tells this story in three cards. The couple enters the union wanting a whole world for two, lives it brightly and in plain sight, and the main task begins when the beautiful image of the partner cracks.

sections.h2: An opera that calls the three cards by name
paragraphs: Wagner wrote Lohengrin entirely himself, words and music; it was first staged in Weimar on 28 August 1850, with Franz Liszt conducting. The plot fits in a few lines. Elsa of Brabant is accused of doing away with her younger brother. She cannot defend herself and tells only a dream: a knight came to her. The king's trumpeters turn to the four quarters of the world and call for a champion. Down the Scheldt comes a knight in silver armour, in a boat drawn by a swan on a golden chain. He defeats the accuser and takes Elsa as his wife on one condition: she must never ask who he is or where he comes from.

The wedding is the next day. The chorus escorts the newlyweds to the bridal chamber and sings (here and below, quotations from the libretto are in our translation): "Fragrant room, adorned for love, now take them in, far from the splendour." The knight sits with Elsa by the window: "We are alone, alone for the first time since we met. Now we have escaped the world." A few minutes later Elsa asks the forbidden question. In the morning, before all the people, the knight names himself — Lohengrin, son of Parzival, knight of the Grail — and sails away.

In the German text the first two cards of the tail have words of their own. Splendour, Glanz, is what the opera calls the radiance of the knight and of the feast. The world, Welt, is everything before whose eyes the story happens. **Both stay outside the bedroom door, and inside, where there is neither world nor splendour, The Tower strikes.** Now, card by card.

sections.h2: The World: "Never shall you ask me"
paragraphs: The World stands at the entry to the task, the point of the couple's shared wishes. In the paid reading the same point appears again, in the sphere "Relationship and common language". This couple's common language is the whole at once. In the opera both of them speak it. At their first meeting Elsa sinks at the knight's feet: "To you I give all that I am." He answers with a condition: "Never shall you ask me, nor trouble yourself to know, whence I sailed here, nor what my name and lineage." And on the wedding night he explains why questions are needless: "We who had never seen each other had divined each other… I had no need to find out your lineage: my eye saw you, and my heart understood you."

In real life this is recognisable at once. The two feel they have always known each other, and the slow stage of getting acquainted is skipped: within a month a shared home, within a year another city or another country, a philosophy for two, private words, their own map of the world. In plus The World gives the couple something rare. One comes home angry and worn out, and the other does not demand that they first become pleasant, but puts the kettle on. They argue at length and out loud, and come out of the argument with an agreement rather than a victory. From outside, such a couple looks like a model.

The resistance grows from the same root. Accept the whole, and there seems to be nothing left to ask about. One says nothing about their former life, their family, their money before the two met, and the other accepts this as the price of the whole. The secrets multiply, the picture of the partner looks less and less like the partner, and the couple stops hearing each other even while talking a great deal.

Benebell Wen describes the hard side of The World (the card drawn reversed) through two states that look like opposites. In the first, the person is "consciously and knowingly in denial" and is "remaining willfully ignorant". The second is "the Great Skeptic", who will "question all, and doubt all". Elsa goes through both in one opera: first an oath to know nothing, then a doubt that within a single day drives her to the question. Ignorance by agreement and suspicion grow from one and the same World, accepted without questions.

In two thirds of these couples The World is made of one partner's The Moon and the other's The Empress, that is, of a dream and of land. Elsa brings the knight exactly this: the dream in which she saw him, and the crown of her father's land — "in my father's lands let him wear the crown". A whole world, given away on the strength of a dream.

sections.h2: The Sun: a life before witnesses
paragraphs: Everything Elsa and the knight live through before the bedroom happens in front of everyone. The trial is held at noon, and the king orders the call: "The sun already stands high at noon — it is time to summon the champion." The crowd looks at the arriving knight and cannot bear to look: "How his armour shines! The eye fails before such splendour!" After the duel both are lifted on shields and carried off amid cheering. In the morning the herald announces the wedding and, in the same breath, a campaign: "Today he celebrates his wedding feast with you, but tomorrow you shall come armed for battle." The bridal procession walks to the cathedral through a living corridor, and Wagner's stage direction specifies that everyone can see Elsa. Only in the bridal chamber are they alone for the first time.

The Sun in the middle of the task shows how the couple travels from the wish to the task. This couple travels it in the light. In readings about love and relationships, Wen calls The Sun "a radiant marriage" and says plainly: "It could suggest a power couple." A home where friends gather. A shared venture they are proud of. Children whose achievements get shared. Together they know how to be a couple in public: they tell one story in two voices, and catch each other's jokes on the fly. In plus each is good at their own work, and one's success does not overshadow the other's: at one partner's award ceremony the other claps loudest, and a month later they swap places.

The difficulty shows in the same scene for anyone who stays to the end of the evening. The guests have gone, the dishes are in the sink, and it turns out there is nothing to talk about, the two of them alone, except plans. Problems go unmentioned so as not to darken the picture. There is so much work that there is no minute for "how are you really": today the wedding, tomorrow the campaign. Expectations rise — of the partner, of oneself, of the union. At an anniversary party one of them tells how "we" built the business, while the other silently counts how many times "I" was said.

In two thirds of these couples The Sun is made of one partner's The Lovers and the other's Death, that is, of a choice and of what was left behind for its sake. Lohengrin speaks of it on the wedding night almost like an accountant: "Your love must richly repay me for what I left behind for you." A light that has a price easily turns into a bill.

sections.h2: The Tower: the question asked in the bedroom
paragraphs: The scene in the bridal chamber is the most exact description of this couple's main task to be found anywhere. In it the question ripens step by step, and a couple can recognise every step.

First Elsa asks for very little — the sound of his name, and only for the two of them: "How sweetly my name slips from your lips! Will you not grant me the sound of yours?.. Alone, when everyone is asleep. The world shall never hear it!" The knight refuses.

Then he reassures her in the language of The Sun: "For I do not come from night and sorrow — I come from splendour and bliss!" It is exactly this that breaks her: "You came to me from bliss, and you long to go back!.. Shall I count the days you still will stay with me?" The radiant image of the partner becomes a source of fear: whoever came from the light will go back to the light.

Then Elsa imagines the swan already swimming to fetch him, and the whole question comes out: "Tell me your name! Whence did you come? What is your lineage?" Lohengrin: "Alas, now all our happiness is gone!" The candles burn down towards dawn.

In the morning comes the denouement, and the opera's main lesson is hidden in it. The truth refused in private, the knight speaks in front of everyone: "Before the whole world, before king and realm, I reveal my secret." First he even accuses his wife for all to hear. **The name that could have been whispered for Elsa alone rings out in the public square, and the marriage ends with it.**

Among the tasks of a couple with The Tower, Yuliana Lisovskaya names three that are acted out in this scene. The collapse of an invented image of the partner — Elsa loved the knight of her dream long before they met. The loss of self-control — the question is asked at the wrong moment and in the wrong way. And the habit of looking in different directions when trouble comes: she looks into the past, at his secret; he looks at the river, where the swan will come for him.

In life the trigger can be anything: a detail from a former life surfaces, someone's status suddenly changes, the one who was always strong is suddenly tired. After a long time in the light, the two meet for the first time without an audience and see an ordinary person where a radiant one used to stand. The hardest thing at that moment is not to sail away on one's own swan: into resentment, into work, into "nobody understands me here".

sections.h2: The Sun and The Tower: one light at different distances
paragraphs: In 1851 Wagner wrote "A Communication to My Friends", in which he explained where Lohengrin came from. He found the outline of the story already among the Greeks: "Who does not know the story of 'Zeus and Semele'?" (in William Ashton Ellis's translation, as are the other quotations from this essay). The god loves a mortal woman and comes to her in human shape. She, "urged by Love's own ardour, demands that her spouse shall show himself to physical sense in the full substance of his being". Zeus knows it will destroy her and still grants the wish — and, Wagner writes, "the fatal splendour of his godlike presence strikes Semele dead".

In the German original that splendour is again Glanz. The very word that in the opera shines on the knight's armour and stays outside the bedroom door kills in Wagner's own account. **The Sun and The Tower in this tail are one and the same light at different distances.** From afar, in public, it warms and dazzles. When it is demanded whole and all at once, at close range, it strikes like lightning.

Running through every date since 1900 turns up one more clue. Neither partner in such a couple has The World or The Sun — not in their personal karmic tail, not in the centre of their personal matrix. The World and The Sun are born only in the sum of the two dates. This couple's radiance is shared: it exists between two people, not in each of them separately. In the opera the knight really did come from the light. In a living couple the light works differently, and in the moment of The Tower each sees the other without the shared radiance — simply because neither has it alone. This is not the unmasking of a fraud. It is meeting a person who until now has only been seen in the light of the couple.

Hence the task. Its point is not that the question must never be asked. The couple needs to learn a third, ordinary light: to see each other neither from afar, as at a celebration, nor in a flash, as on the night of the question, but by day, piece by piece, without demanding that everything be shown at once.

The usual moral of this story is "she should have trusted and not asked". Wagner himself thought otherwise. In the same "Communication" he writes that he found Elsa "so justified in the final outburst of her jealousy" that this very outburst taught him "the purely-human element of love". He describes her question as the moment she "wakes first from out the thrill of worship into the full reality of Love". And he admits that Elsa "made me a Revolutionary at one blow".

One more detail from the same text. "Infected", as he puts it, "with the doubting spirit of Criticism", Wagner sketched a different ending: Lohengrin, once revealed, would "put aside his higher nature" in favour of "a sojourn upon earth with Elsa". He then rejected it as "utterly unsatisfactory" and "unnatural", and put the knight back in the boat.

Wagner's source, Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival (early thirteenth century), tells the same story in fewer than a hundred lines, and more calmly. There the Duchess of Brabant does not even have a name. Before all the people the knight sets his condition: "Never ask who I am — then I can stay with you" (our translation from Middle High German, as below). He becomes a good judge, "together they had fine children", and only then does the question come. He leaves, in Wolfram's word, "unwillingly", and leaves behind a sword, a horn and a little ring. Wolfram judges more harshly than Wagner: the knight had warned her, after all, when he came to her out of the sea.

Eight centuries lie between the two verdicts, and a couple with this tail needs both. From Wagner, the right to ask: Elsa's question is not a sin of curiosity but a step from worship to a living person. From Wolfram, the years and the children between the oath and the question — that is, a Sun lived long enough for there to be something to protect. In plus, Lisovskaya's Tower sounds like this: trials gone through together make the union stronger, and in sudden trouble the two calmly hold on to each other. **The ending Wagner sketched and rejected — the knight said his name and stayed — is exactly this couple's main task.**

sections.h2: The Hierophant in the centre: the rule about what may be shown
paragraphs: A couple with tail 21-19-16 always has the same centre — The Hierophant, the fifth arcanum, in 100% of such couples. In two thirds of them it is made of the personal centres 12 and 20 (The Hanged Man and Judgement), in the rest of 7 and 16 (The Chariot and The Tower).

Waite describes The Hierophant's gesture: with his raised right hand he gives a sign "distinguishing between the manifest and concealed part of doctrine". The opera knows this rule. Telling the story of the Grail, Lohengrin explains why he kept silent: "So sublime is the Grail's blessing that, once revealed, it must flee the layman's eye." The knight is not secretive by nature — he serves a rule under which one thing may be shown and another may not. Waite also warns about the danger of this card: "it may so happen that the pontiff forgets the significance of this his symbolic state and acts as if he contained within his proper measures all that his sign signifies". Then the rule starts living in place of the people.

The couple's centre is its atmosphere, what happens between the two when nobody is watching. For this couple The Hierophant lives there. In plus this is a couple with its own holidays and its own order: a Sunday breakfast that is never cancelled, a word that is kept, and decisions that one partner makes for both with the other's full consent. And the partners remain friends. In minus the same Hierophant gives lectures: one knows how things should be done and patiently remakes the other, and the couple's door is closed to everyone, sometimes even to the partners themselves. For tail 21-19-16 what matters most is which rule sits in the centre. "We don't quarrel in front of guests" protects both. "In our house we don't talk about your parents" hides something, and rules like that store up the question to come.

sections.h2: The couple's values: the swan's golden chain
paragraphs: In the sphere "The couple's values" such couples have The Devil (78.6%) or The Lovers (21.4%).

The swan that brings the knight draws the boat on a golden chain. In the finale Ortrud, the sorceress and Elsa's chief enemy, gloats: by the little chain she herself wound around the swan, she knew who it was — Elsa's lost brother, the heir of Brabant. Lohengrin takes the chain off the swan, and a boy rises from the river. The radiance came to Brabant drawn by an enchanted chain.

Waite himself links The Devil with The Hierophant. The Devil's raised hand is "the reverse of that benediction which is given by the Hierophant in the fifth card", and the two chained figures at his feet "are analogous with those of the fifth card". The chain, for Waite, is "the chain and fatality of the material life". In the couple's centre there is a blessing; in its values, the same blessing turned inside out. In plus, The Devil in the values is a passion nobody is ashamed of: the two know each other's dark sides and say their wishes out loud, even the awkward ones. In minus it is the wish to own: to check, to hold on, to tie the other down with money or status — and silence about what one really wants. The closing thought of Lisovskaya's section on The Devil deserves to hang over this couple's door: nobody belongs to anybody. Lohengrin takes the chain off only after The Tower. The couple would do well to take it off sooner.
Where the values hold The Lovers, the value becomes the choice itself: the union rests not on an oath given once by a river, but on a decision the two keep making again.

sections.h2: The Sun instead of the Wheel: how tail 21-19-16 is worked out
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22. Example: the dates 04.07.1975 and 04.01.1976. The first partner's personal tail is 18-6-6, the second's is 3-13-10.
The couple's centre: 12 + 20 = 32 → 3 + 2 = 5, The Hierophant. "The couple's values" in this example are 15, The Devil.

The couple's middle is not recalculated from the ends. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is the sum of its ends: 21 + 16 = 37 → 10, The Wheel of Fortune. That is why 21-19-16 never occurs as a personal tail. For a couple the middle is added up from the two personal middles: 6 + 13 = 19.

Here is one more clue. A personal middle is the sum of its own ends, so a couple's middle always reduces to the same digit as the sum of its ends: 37 → 10 → 1. Of the numbers up to 22, only 10 and 19 reduce to one, and one itself never appears in a couple. So a couple that enters the task through The World and works on The Tower can only have The Wheel or The Sun in the middle. The Wheel comes up in one couple in 107 — that is tail 21-10-16. The Sun comes up in one in 1,572 (0.064%, 87th place of 97 couple tails). Among couples with these ends, roughly one in sixteen gets The Sun.

The Sun appears only when the partners' middles add up to exactly 19 without reduction: 6 + 13 (personal tails 18-6-6 and 3-13-10, 66% of such couples) or 5 + 14 (15-5-8 and 6-14-8, 34%). Tails 3-13-10 and 6-14-8 are among the rarest personal tails: since 1900 they have fallen on 149 and 55 birth dates, almost all between January and April. Hence the rarity.

What this means. Almost every couple with the same entry and the same main task has The Wheel in the middle: life turns now up, now down, and reminds them by itself that luck changes. This couple has The Sun at its height where The Wheel would stand. Luck seems to have stopped at noon, "the sun already stands high", and The Wheel's lesson — everything changes — arrives all at once, through The Tower.
This tail has no permutations: the numbers 21, 19 and 16 in any other order do not form a couple tail.

sections.h2: How to live tail 21-19-16 in plus

ul: **Ask by daylight.** Do not save up "who are you really" until the night after a celebration, but ask a little at a time on ordinary days, when the answer breaks nothing. In the opera the question is asked at night, by guttering candles, and the answer is given in full daylight — when it is already too late.

**Answer in private.** If the partner asks for a truth meant for the two of them only, that is the best form a question can take. Refusing it, as Lohengrin does, usually ends with the truth told in front of everyone.
**Review the rules in the centre.** Every so often, go through the couple's own "we don't do that here" together and separate the rules that protect from the rules that hide.
**Keep the collapse out of the public square.** No judging each other in front of friends, family or followers. The Tower is a matter for two.

**Check the image against the person.** Each names honestly what in the partner they invented themselves and what they saw with their own eyes. The invented part is not the partner's lie but one's own dream, and the dreamer answers for it.
**Share The Sun.** Tell the couple's success as a shared one, and do not take the other's part for oneself.
**Stay after the name.** When the truth has been spoken, do not step into the boat. Wagner turned down the ending where the knight stays, but nothing stops a couple from writing it.

**The World (21), entry to the task.** The shared wish is to accept each other at once and entirely, without questions, as if the partner had arrived ready-made from a distant land. The same wish turns into resistance when "don't ask" becomes a rule.

**The Sun (19), middle of the task.** The couple travels its road in the light: celebrations, successes, a home open to friends, and everyone around saying "the perfect couple". In plain sight it is easy to love an image, because everyone can see it, the partners included.

**The Tower (16), main task.** To live through the moment when the two are alone for the first time, with no audience and no radiance, and ask each other "who are you?" — and then not to part, but to build again, this time on the truth.

intro: The tail does not predict a break-up or a disaster. It describes a plot that each couple lives with its own force and in its own time. The roles in this plot are not split by sex: either partner may stay silent or ask, and they often swap places.

faq.q: Is karmic tail 21-19-16 in compatibility a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail describes tasks, not a verdict. The World at the entry gives this couple a rare ability to accept each other whole, The Sun in the middle gives warmth, success and respect. The Tower shows where all this wealth needs a foundation: in truth told in time.

faq.q: Does The Tower in a couple's tail mean the couple will split up?
faq.a: No. The Tower as the main task describes the collapse of an invented image of the partner and of the couple, not an event with a date. In plus, Lisovskaya links it to trials gone through together, after which the union is stronger. One can part with the image and stay with the person.

faq.q: How does tail 21-19-16 differ from tail 21-10-16?
faq.a: They share the entry, The World, and the main task, The Tower, but the middles differ. In 21-10-16 the middle is The Wheel: the couple's life turns, and changes come gradually. In 21-19-16 the middle is The Sun: the couple lives in a long noon, and change comes all at once, as a blow. The second tail is almost fifteen times rarer.

faq.q: Can one person have karmic tail 21-19-16?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail equals the sum of its ends, and 21 + 16 give 10, The Wheel. The triple 21-19-16 exists only for a couple, because its middle is added up from the middles of the two partners.

faq.q: Who in the couple is Elsa, and who is Lohengrin?
faq.a: Either of the two, and more often by turns. In one situation a partner arrives "from splendour" and asks not to be questioned; in another the same partner saves up a question and asks it at the wrong moment. Sex decides nothing here.

unit.meaning: Your task is to see each other without the shared radiance and to stay together once the truth has been spoken.
